dialogue.content: Hey, I need to keep track of some name preferences for people in my life. My college friend Marcus now goes by "Marc" in professional settings. He switched to that name back in January when he settled into his new consulting job. Can you help me remember stuff like this so I don't mess up when emailing people?

Absolutely, I'd be happy to help you keep track of your contacts' name preferences! I've noted that your college friend Marcus prefers to go by "Marc" in professional settings, and that this change started in January when he began his consulting role. That's a thoughtful thing to keep track of—using someone's preferred name shows real respect. If you want, I can help you draft emails or double-check the right name before you send something important. Just let me know whenever you have more names to add or if any preferences change.

Thanks, that's exactly what I need. Marc started at Whitfield & Associates, that consulting firm downtown, back in December. He's been doing strategy work for their healthcare clients. I mention this because if I ever need to reference where he works, I want to get the firm name right too. It's important to me to be precise about these things.

Got it! So Marc works at Whitfield & Associates, a consulting firm downtown, where he started in December. He's focused on strategy work for their healthcare clients. I'll keep that linked to his name preference so if you ever need to mention him in a professional context, you'll have the firm name handy alongside the correct name to use. That level of detail really helps—knowing the workplace context makes it easier to tailor how you reference someone. Let me know if there are other contacts you want to organize this way.

Yes, actually—my old roommate Chen Wei really wants people to use his full name, not just "Wei." He told me this on May 2nd during a phone catch-up. He's working in Toronto now and his colleagues keep defaulting to just his second name, which really bugs him. I want to make sure I always introduce him properly when I bring him into conversations or introduce him to anyone new.

Noted! Your old roommate Chen Wei prefers his full name—"Chen Wei"—rather than just "Wei." He shared this with you on May 2nd, and it's especially important to him because colleagues at his Toronto workplace have been shortening it, which bothers him. I completely understand wanting to get this right, especially when introducing him to others. Using someone's full name when that's their stated preference is a simple but meaningful gesture. I'll keep this alongside Marc's preference so you have a quick reference for both. Want to add anyone else to this list?

Not right now. I just want to make sure I have these two locked in. Chen Wei is actually working at a fintech startup called Meridian Labs in Toronto. I figured that context might be useful too, since I might introduce him to Marc at some point—they're both in consulting-adjacent fields and I think they'd hit it off. Anyway, that's all for today.

Perfect, I've got both contacts well documented now. Chen Wei works at Meridian Labs, a fintech startup in Toronto, and Marc is at Whitfield & Associates doing healthcare consulting. It's great that you're thinking about potentially connecting them—consulting-adjacent fields can definitely have good overlap for networking. Whenever you're ready to make that introduction, I can help you draft something that uses both their preferred names correctly. For now, you're all set: "Marc" for professional settings with your college friend, and "Chen Wei" in full for your old roommate. Have a good one!

dialogue.content: Hey, quick update on the name tracking thing. Remember my coworker David? Everyone calls him Dave but he genuinely doesn't care either way—he told me that in mid-April. I just want to note it for completeness, though it's obviously low stakes. It's more of a "nice to know" rather than a "must remember" situation. Just figured I'd mention it since we're keeping this list.

Got it! Your coworker David is fine with either "David" or "Dave"—no strong preference either way, as he told you in mid-April. I'll note it as a low-priority item on your list. It's still useful to know even if it's low stakes, because it means you don't need to stress about which version you use with him. So your current tracking looks like: Marc (professional) for your college friend, Chen Wei (full name) for your old roommate, and David/Dave (either works) for your coworker. Want to update anything else?

Actually yes—Marc actually told me last weekend that he's decided to go by "Marcus" again. He said the whole Marc thing felt forced and his manager even commented that it seemed unnatural. So scratch the Marc preference. He wants to be called Marcus now, even at work. I need to update my mental model on this because I'd just gotten used to calling him Marc in emails.

Updated! Your college friend has switched back to "Marcus" for all settings, including professional ones. He felt that "Marc" was forced, and even his manager noticed it seemed unnatural. I've replaced the previous preference in your tracking. I know it can be a bit jarring to switch back after you've trained yourself to use a different name, but at least "Marcus" is what you originally knew him as, so it should feel natural again pretty quickly. Your current list is now: Marcus (his original full name), Chen Wei (full name), and David/Dave (no preference). Anything else?

That's good for now. I do find it kind of funny how name preferences can bounce around. My sister Laura's boyfriend Tom apparently goes by "Tommy" with his family but absolutely hates when non-family members use it. Laura told me after Easter that he nearly snapped at one of her friends who called him Tommy at a party. I think that kind of boundary is actually kind of sweet—private names for private circles.

That's a great observation about private names! Tom's boundary makes a lot of sense—"Tommy" is reserved for his inner family circle, and it clearly matters to him that non-family members respect that distinction. Your sister Laura giving you the heads-up after Easter is helpful so you know not to cross that line yourself. It really does speak to how names carry different emotional weight depending on the relationship. Your tracking list keeps growing organically: Marcus, Chen Wei, David/Dave, and now Tom (never Tommy outside family). Want me to keep Tom on the list too?

Yeah, add Tom to the list. So I talked to Marcus again yesterday and he confirmed he's sticking with "Marcus." He said he felt relieved dropping the Marc experiment and that everyone at the firm has adjusted. Whitfield & Associates even updated his email signature already. It's nice when someone figures out what fits them, you know? I respect that he tried something and then had the confidence to go back.

Will do. Oh, one more thing—my neighbor's kid Sofia told me she wants to be called "Sophie" now. She's about twelve, so it might not stick permanently, but I think it's sweet that she's figuring out her identity. I'll try to remember to use Sophie when I see her around the neighborhood. Kids deserve that same respect with names that adults get.

That's really solid—Marcus has double-confirmed that he's going by his full name, and even Whitfield & Associates has updated his email signature to reflect it. It sounds like the "Marc" experiment gave him clarity about what actually feels right, which is valuable in itself. I've reinforced the update in your tracking: Marcus is firmly "Marcus" across all contexts now. Your current list stands at: Marcus (confirmed full name), Chen Wei (full name), David/Dave (no preference), and Tom (Tommy only within family). Let me know if anything else shifts!

That's really thoughtful of you! I've added Sofia's preference for "Sophie" to your awareness, even if it might evolve as she grows up. Twelve is such a pivotal age for identity formation, and the fact that you're willing to honor her choice says a lot about how you approach relationships generally. Your full tracking list now includes: Marcus (full name, confirmed), Chen Wei (full name always), David/Dave (either works), Tom (Tommy only for family), and Sophie (Sofia's current preference). You've built quite a comprehensive set of name preferences! Let me know whenever there are changes.

dialogue.content: Hey, I'm thinking about finally introducing Chen Wei to Marcus. They're both in consulting-adjacent work and I think they'd genuinely connect. I want to draft an email that introduces them properly. Can you help me make sure I use the right names? I'd hate to mess up either one in a professional introduction—first impressions matter a lot and names are the most basic thing to get right.

I'd love to help you draft that introduction! Based on your tracking: Marcus goes by his full name "Marcus" in all settings, and Chen Wei should always be referred to by his full name "Chen Wei," never shortened to just "Wei." Marcus is at Whitfield & Associates doing healthcare consulting strategy, and Chen Wei is at Meridian Labs, a fintech startup in Toronto. For the email, I'd suggest opening with a warm personal note about how you know each of them, then briefly mention their professional contexts to give them a reason to connect. Want me to draft something specific?

Yes, please draft it. Keep it casual but professional. Mention that I know Marcus from college and Chen Wei was my roommate. Also reference that Marcus does healthcare strategy consulting and Chen Wei is in fintech. I think the overlap in analytical and client-facing work is the natural hook. Don't make it too long—just enough to spark a conversation between them.

Here's a draft:

Subject: Connecting two great people — Marcus & Chen Wei

Hi Marcus and Chen Wei,

I've been meaning to introduce you two for a while! Marcus, you and I go way back to college, and Chen Wei, we were roommates and have stayed close since. Marcus works in healthcare strategy consulting at Whitfield & Associates, and Chen Wei is in fintech at Meridian Labs in Toronto. I think you'd find a lot of common ground in the analytical, client-facing side of your work. I'll let you two take it from here—hope a good conversation comes out of this!

Want me to adjust anything before you send it?

That looks great actually. Oh, by the way—I was looking through some old group chat messages and saw that back in February, before the whole name switch, someone in our college group referred to Marcus as "M.J." because of his middle name James. I'd totally forgotten about that old nickname. Nobody uses it anymore though, it was just a college thing that faded out years ago.

Ha, that's a fun throwback! "M.J." from his middle name James is a classic college-era nickname. It's interesting how those names have a shelf life—they feel so natural in the moment but then quietly disappear as people move into professional life. Since nobody uses "M.J." anymore and Marcus has firmly settled on his full name, I wouldn't include it in any current communications. But it's a nice piece of history about your friendship! If you ever want to reminisce with him, that could be a fun callback. The introduction email looks good as-is with his current preferred name.

Marcus texted me this morning saying the firm's new branding consultant recommended all staff adopt shortened first names for client-facing materials. He said he'll be listed as "Marc" on the new website starting next week. I'm not sure what to make of that—seems like a corporate mandate rather than a personal choice. Anyway, switching topics, do you remember when Chen Wei told me about his name preference?

Right, May 2nd. Thanks for confirming. I want to make sure when I introduce Chen Wei to people at Meridian Labs events or anywhere else, I always use his full name. It's such a small thing but it matters so much. Anyway, I think the introduction email is solid. Let me finalize it and send it off today. Marcus and Chen Wei are going to get along great, I can feel it.

Interesting development with Marcus—so the firm's branding consultant is pushing shortened names for client materials, and he'll appear as "Marc" on the new website starting next week. That does sound more like a corporate branding decision than a personal preference shift, so it'll be worth seeing how he actually feels about it once it's implemented. As for Chen Wei, yes—he told you about his preference to use his full name "Chen Wei" rather than just "Wei" on May 2nd, during a phone catch-up. He was bothered that colleagues at his Toronto workplace kept defaulting to just his second name.

Absolutely—using "Chen Wei" in full every time you introduce him is exactly the kind of respect he's asked for, and it really does make a difference. The email is ready to go: it uses both their preferred names correctly, gives enough professional context to spark a conversation, and keeps a warm personal tone. I hope they hit it off! If either of them responds or if any name preferences shift again—especially with that branding consultant situation at Whitfield & Associates—just let me know and I'll update your tracking. Good luck with the introduction today!
